title: Approbation of a comprehensive time-to-contact test: Factors influencing task performance
abstract: Context and relevance. The ability to extrapolate movement is the basis for successful interaction with dynamically changing objects in the environment. To perform such tasks, individuals may rely on either cognitive motion extrapolation or cognitive clocking based on a previously estimated time interval. Objective: to probe a comprehensive implementation of time-to-contact tasks aimed at assessing the ability to extrapolate movement, to evaluate the effect of the implemented task types on response accuracy, and to study the effect of learning on task performance. Methods and materials. The study sample consisted of six people aged 32 to 44 years. Participants completed an experimental protocol consisting of different types of tasks in the morning and evening hours for at least 5 days (total number of measurements 10 to 28, M = 21.83, SD = 8.21). The task included seven levels reflecting different aspects of experimental tasks on extrapolation of movement. From level to level, the complexity of the movement trajectory, the ability to track movement (hiding the trajectory or its part), as well as orientation to the timing (fixed time of the ball's movement) sequentially varied. Results. Task performance accuracy varied significantly between the implemented levels, with the greatest difficulty being caused by complicating the movement trajectory and concealing it, while the fixed duration of the object’ movement did not facilitate task performance. No learning effect was observed across multiple test repetitions during the study. Conclusions. The results indicate the leading role of the motion tracking mechanism, rather than the timing strategy, in the success of extrapolation. The proposed paradigm provides a sensitive tool for studying the cognitive mechanisms of contact time estimation.
